questions.prompt: In an undisturbed stack of sedimentary rock layers, where are the older layers generally found?
questions.accessiblePrompt: In an undisturbed stack of sedimentary rock layers, where are the older layers generally found?
questions.conditions: Undisturbed means the layers have not been folded, flipped over, or moved since they formed.

choices.text: Below the younger layers
choices.rationale: Correct. Each new layer settles on top of what is already there, so in an undisturbed stack the layers get older as you go down.

choices.text: Above the younger layers
choices.rationale: This flips the order. A layer can only settle on top of layers that already exist, so the upper layers are the newer ones.

choices.text: In whichever layer is thickest
choices.rationale: Thickness depends on how much sediment piled up, not on when the layer formed. A thin layer can be older than a thick one.

choices.text: In whichever layer is darkest
choices.rationale: Color comes from what the rock is made of, such as iron minerals or plant remains. It is not a reliable clue to age.

questions.explanation: This is the law of superposition. Sediment settles in layers, each one on top of the last, so in an undisturbed stack the bottom layer formed first and the top layer formed last. That is why geologists read rock layers from the bottom up.
questions.misconception: The top layer is oldest because it has been exposed longest, or thicker or darker layers are older.
questions.hint: Think of mail piling up on a table all week. Where is Monday's mail?

questions.prompt: No one watched the lower sedimentary layers of the Grand Canyon form. Why can geologists still use superposition to say those layers are older than the ones above them?
questions.accessiblePrompt: No one was there to watch the lower sedimentary layers of the Grand Canyon form. Why can geologists still use superposition to say that those layers are older than the layers above them?

choices.text: They assume sediment settled long ago the same way it settles today.
choices.rationale: Correct. Geologists can watch sediment settle in layers today, and they assume the same natural laws worked the same way in the past. That assumption lets them read layers no one saw form.

choices.text: Scientists long ago watched those layers form and wrote down the order.
choices.rationale: Those layers formed hundreds of millions of years before any people lived, so no one could have watched them. The order comes from reasoning, not from eyewitnesses.

choices.text: Deep rock ages faster because of the heat and pressure underground.
choices.rationale: Heat and pressure can squeeze and harden buried sediment, but they can't change when a layer was laid down. Age depends on the time of deposition.

choices.text: The lower layers are harder, and harder rock takes longer to form.
choices.rationale: Hardness depends on what a rock is made of and how well it was cemented, not on its age. A soft layer can be older than a hard one.

questions.explanation: Superposition rests on an assumption: the natural laws at work today, such as gravity pulling sediment down into layers, worked the same way in the past and everywhere on Earth. Geologists state that assumption and check the conditions that go with it, such as whether the layers have been overturned. Then the lower layers can be read as older, even though no one saw them form.
questions.misconception: The order of rock layers can be known only if someone saw them form, or deep layers are older because burial makes rock age faster.
questions.hint: Think about what geologists can watch happening today at a river mouth or a beach.

questions.prompt: Sort each finding by the kind of dating it comes from.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sort each finding into one of two groups: relative dating, which puts events in order without giving years, or absolute dating, which gives an approximate age in years.

items.text: In this undisturbed cliff, the fossil bed lies 30 meters below the ash layer, so it is older.
items.rationale: Relative: 30 meters is a distance, not an age. The bed's position shows only that it came first, not how many years ago.

items.text: This volcanic ash erupted about 75 million years ago.
items.rationale: Absolute: it gives an approximate age in years, which takes radiometric dating.

items.text: The dike is younger than the sandstone it cuts.
items.rationale: Relative: cross-cutting tells which came first, not how long ago.

items.text: Measuring uranium and lead in a zircon crystal shows how many years ago it formed.
items.rationale: Absolute: measuring radioactive atoms and their decay products gives an age in years.

items.text: Shales in two states hold the same index fossil, so they are about the same age.
items.rationale: Relative: matching fossils shows the layers formed in the same span of time, without giving years.

items.text: A lava flow is 1.1 billion years old, give or take a few million years.
items.rationale: Absolute: an age in years with an uncertainty is a result of absolute dating.

questions.explanation: Relative dating answers "which came first?" using superposition, cross-cutting features and fossils. Absolute dating answers "about how many years ago?" by measuring radioactive atoms, mostly in igneous rock. Geologists use both together.
questions.misconception: Any finding that contains a number, or any statement about age, counts as absolute dating; or fossils give ages in years.
questions.hint: For each finding, ask which question it answers: "Which came first?" or "About how many years ago?"

questions.prompt: In an undisturbed cliff, a sandstone layer sits directly on top of a shale layer. Using only this observation, which claim is supported?

choices.text: The sandstone is younger, but not by a known number of years.
choices.rationale: Correct. The sandstone was laid down after the shale, but its position alone can't measure the time between them.

choices.text: The sandstone is about 10 million years younger than the shale.
choices.rationale: Nothing in the observation gives a number of years. A stack shows order; putting a number on the gap would take absolute dating.

choices.text: The two layers formed at the same time, because they touch.
choices.rationale: Touching layers can be separated by a little time or a lot. Superposition still says the upper one was laid down later.

choices.text: The shale is younger, because softer rock forms faster.
choices.rationale: How fast a rock forms doesn't change which layer was laid down first. The upper layer, the sandstone, is the younger one.

questions.explanation: Superposition gives a relative age: the sandstone was deposited after the shale. It can't tell whether the gap between them was a week or millions of years. Turning order into years takes absolute dating, usually of nearby igneous rock.
questions.misconception: Relative dating can tell how many years apart two layers formed.
questions.hint: Does a stack of layers come with a calendar? What does its order tell you, and what doesn't it?

questions.prompt: Jamal finds a limestone layer 20 meters below the top of a canyon wall. He says, "Layers build up about 1 meter every million years, so this limestone is 20 million years old." What is the best response?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Jamal finds a limestone layer 20 meters below the top of a canyon wall. He says: layers build up about 1 meter every million years, so this limestone is 20 million years old. What is the best response to his claim?

choices.text: Depth shows order, not years: rates vary, and erosion can remove layers.
choices.rationale: Correct. A meter of mud might settle quickly in a flood or very slowly in a calm sea, and erosion can wipe out layers entirely. Position tells which is older; years need absolute dating.

choices.text: He is right, since all sediment piles up at one steady rate everywhere.
choices.rationale: Sediment builds up fast in some places and times and slowly in others, and sometimes stops while erosion removes rock. There's no single rate to use.

choices.text: He should count the layers instead, since each layer stands for a million years.
choices.rationale: Layers aren't a set amount of time each. One layer may form in a day; another may take many thousands of years.

choices.text: He is right if all the rock above it is limestone too.
choices.rationale: Even limestone can build up quickly in some stretches of time and slowly in others, and erosion can remove layers of any kind. Rock type alone does not turn depth into years.

questions.explanation: Superposition says the limestone is older than the layers above it, but depth is not a clock. Sediment doesn't pile up at one set pace, and some stretches of time leave no layer at all because erosion removed it. Scientists get ages in years from radiometric dating of igneous rock.
questions.misconception: Depth or thickness of rock converts directly into years.
questions.hint: What would have to be true about every meter of this rock for Jamal's math to work? Can the cliff alone show that?

questions.prompt: On both sides of a river canyon, the same red, tan and gray layers appear in the same order and with the same thicknesses. What does the principle of lateral continuity let you conclude about the red layer on the two sides?
questions.accessiblePrompt: On both sides of a river canyon, the same red, tan and gray layers appear in the same order and with the same thicknesses. What does the principle of lateral continuity let you conclude about the red layer on the two sides of the canyon?

choices.text: It is one layer of the same age, later cut through by the river.
choices.rationale: Correct. Matching layers in the same position were laid down as one continuous sheet during the same span of time, and erosion later split it.

choices.text: The red layer on the higher side of the canyon is older.
choices.rationale: Which side stands higher doesn't change when the layer formed. Matching layers in the same place in the sequence formed together.

choices.text: The river laid down a separate red layer on each side after carving the canyon.
choices.rationale: The canyon cuts through the layers, so the layers came first. A river carving a canyon removes rock rather than building matching layers on both walls.

choices.text: Each side's red layer formed at a different time, since a canyon divides them.
choices.rationale: The gap came later, from erosion. Before the river cut down, the layer stretched straight across.

questions.explanation: Sediment spreads out sideways in a layer until something stops it. When matching layers show up on both sides of a gap, they were one continuous layer that weathering and erosion later cut through. So the red layer is the same age on both sides, and the canyon is younger than all the layers it slices through.
questions.misconception: Layers separated by a canyon formed separately or at different times.
questions.hint: Which came first: the layers, or the canyon that cuts them?

questions.prompt: A tan layer shows up on both sides of a wide valley. Which observations would support the idea that the two parts were once one continuous layer? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: A tan layer shows up on both sides of a wide valley. Which observations would support the idea that the two parts were once one continuous layer? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Both parts match in rock type, color and thickness.
choices.rationale: Correct. Matching rock type, color and thickness suggest the same sediment settled in one continuous sheet.

choices.text: Both parts have the same layers above and below them.
choices.rationale: Correct. Sitting in the same place in the sequence is strong evidence the parts formed together.

choices.text: The valley between the two parts is very deep.
choices.rationale: A deep valley shows a lot of erosion happened, but it says nothing about whether the two parts match.

choices.text: Both parts contain fossils of some kind.
choices.rationale: Many layers hold fossils. Only the same species, in the same place in the sequence, would link the two parts; fossils of any kind don't.

choices.text: Both parts have cracks running through them.
choices.rationale: Cracks can form in almost any rock long after it hardens, so sharing cracks doesn't show the two parts were once one layer.

questions.explanation: To argue that layers were once connected, geologists look for matching features: the same rock type, color and thickness, and the same place in the sequence of layers. When several clues line up, the best explanation is one layer that erosion later cut apart.
questions.misconception: Any feature of the landscape counts as evidence that two layers match.
questions.hint: Which clues would be unlikely to match by chance if the two parts were different layers?

questions.prompt: A road cut shows layers of shale and limestone tilted steeply, like books leaning on a shelf. What does the principle of original horizontality tell you about them?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A road cut shows layers of shale and limestone tilted steeply, like books leaning on a shelf. What does the principle of original horizontality tell you about these layers?
questions.limitations: Sediment can settle on gentle slopes, such as the front of a delta, but whole layers of mud and lime tilted steeply like these point to later movement.

choices.text: They were laid down flat, then tilted later by forces inside Earth.
choices.rationale: Correct. Sediment settles in flat or nearly flat layers, so a steep tilt means the layers were moved after they formed.

choices.text: The ground tilted first, and then the mud settled into a tilted shape.
choices.rationale: Loose mud can't rest in layers this steep; on sloping ground it slides downhill and fills in toward flat layers. Layers tilted this steeply were moved after they formed.

choices.text: These tilted layers are younger than the flat layers in a nearby hill.
choices.rationale: The tilt shows only that the tilting came after these layers formed. It can't compare their age with layers somewhere else.

choices.text: Digging the road cut tipped the layers over.
choices.rationale: Digging exposes the layers, but it can't tip thick layers of solid bedrock. The tilt was already there, made long before by slow tectonic forces.

questions.explanation: Gravity makes sediment settle in flat or nearly flat layers. So when sedimentary layers are steeply tilted or folded, something happened to them after they formed, usually slow, powerful pushing from colliding tectonic plates. The layers are older than the tilting.
questions.misconception: Sedimentary layers can form already tilted, or the tilt was caused by something recent such as digging.
questions.hint: How does mud settle when it sinks through calm water?

questions.prompt: In a tightly folded mountain, part of a fold has flipped completely over. Which statement about the layers in the flipped part is correct?
questions.accessiblePrompt: In a tightly folded mountain, part of a fold has been flipped completely upside down. Which statement about the layers in the flipped part is correct?

choices.text: The oldest layer is now on top of the younger ones.
choices.rationale: Correct. In the overturned part the stack reads upside down, so the layer that formed first now lies on top of the younger layers.

choices.text: The bottom layer must still be the oldest one.
choices.rationale: Superposition reads straight up only when layers are right-side up. Where a fold has flipped the stack, the bottom layer is now the youngest.

choices.text: Folding changed the layers' ages along with their order.
choices.rationale: Folding moves layers but can't change when they formed. Each layer keeps its age; only its position changes.

choices.text: The folding happened before the layers were laid down.
choices.rationale: The layers had to exist before they could be bent, so the folding is younger than the layers.

questions.explanation: Superposition reads bottom-to-top only when layers are undisturbed or at least right-side up. Tectonic forces can bend layers so far that part of a stack ends up on its side or upside down. In those places, geologists first work out how the layers were folded, then read their order.
questions.misconception: The bottom layer is always the oldest, even where layers have been flipped over.
questions.hint: Superposition has a condition built in. Does a flipped fold meet it?

choices.text: Layer A formed before layer F.
choices.rationale: Correct. With no sign of overturning, superposition still applies along the tilted stack: the lowest layer, A, formed first.

choices.text: The layers were tilted after they formed.
choices.rationale: Correct. Sea-floor sand and lime settle in flat or nearly flat layers, so a tilt shared by the whole stack came later.

choices.rationale: Correct. Fossils of sea animals in sandstone and limestone show those layers formed on a sea floor.

choices.text: B and F formed at the same time, since both are volcanic.
choices.rationale: Layers of the same rock type can form at very different times. Here other layers lie between B and F, so B is older.

choices.text: Each layer took the same number of years to form.
